name: Sara Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep a routine, because otherwise the days blur. I write a to-do list at breakfast, spend the morning on applications and a medical-terminology course online, then walk to my mum's for lunch since she lives ten minutes away. Until May I was the receptionist and office coordinator at Greenacre Dental in Eldermoor, nine years. A dental group bought the practice and moved bookings and billing to a central team, so the front desk went. I live in a one-bed flat above a hairdresser's and I'm on benefits only.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the version I'd bet on, with some caution. A bit of automation here and there, and everything else carrying on much as before. I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most tools, handy in places and overrated in others. I'd tell friends to try it where it helps, such as for drafting letters, and not to panic. I'd also say that companies cutting staff will blame whatever is fashionable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry isn't AI. It's that small practices keep being bought up and the work moved to some central team. That was my job, and that trend continues whether AI is hype or not. So I'm worried about getting hired in the same kind of role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the medical-terminology course, which leads to a certificate in medical administration, in about ten weeks. I'd apply to GP surgeries, the hospital outpatient department and a couple of private clinics, about eight a week. I'd use a chatbot now and then to tidy a cover letter, but I'd rewrite it in my own voice before sending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady on the surface, jittery underneath. The rent is due on the first and it's covered by my benefits, but just. I check my balance more often than I'd admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check when you check your balance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the housing payment's landed and whether there's enough for the electric top-up. I split my money into envelopes in my head: rent, electric, food, travel, and a small one for the unexpected, which is usually empty. When it's empty, my mum slips me twenty pounds and pretends it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rewrite the chatbot's letter in your own voice. What's different in your voice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm plain. The chatbot loves words like 'passionate' and 'dynamic', and I'd never say those about a dental waiting room. I'd say I kept three hundred patients calm and every appointment on time, which is true and sounds like me.

say: I'd say AI is **handy in places**, overrated in others, and companies blame whatever is fashionable.
I'd tell friends to try it for drafting **letters** and not panic.
think: My worry is **small practices** being bought up and the work moved to a central team.
That trend continues whether AI is **hype or not**.
do: Finish the medical-terminology course and get the **certificate** in about ten weeks.
Apply to GP surgeries, outpatient departments and private clinics, about **eight a week**.
Use a chatbot to tidy a cover letter and **rewrite** it in my own voice.
feel: Steady on the surface and **jittery** underneath, checking my balance more often than I'd admit.
S0.quote: I kept three hundred patients calm and every appointment on time, which is true and sounds like me.
fieldNote: Splits money into **mental envelopes**, and the unexpected one is usually empty.

Anxious because her kind of role is the one being centralised.

steps.text: Finish the medical-terminology course and sit the exam in ten weeks
Apply to eight GP surgeries and clinics a week
Use a chatbot to draft cover letters and rewrite them in my own words
Keep the weekly lunch and to-do list routine at my mum's

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one is closer to my own experience. Booking, answering customers, checking and billing are the things the dental group moved to its central team, and I can see them going to software soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift, and we should be honest about who it hits first, which is admin and front-desk workers. I'd say the government should fund retraining with a stipend and not just a leaflet. I'd tell my friends in office jobs to learn the tools before their boss does it for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think receptionist and coordinator jobs will get thinner each year, and the ones left will be harder to land. I'd be applying against people who have the same experience plus the same retraining. Still, I'm not hopeless, because clinics need someone who can calm a frightened patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to roles that mix admin with patient contact, like clinical support worker or practice coordinator in a health setting. I'd take a short course on the practice-management software, and I'd start using AI tools for scheduling and drafting, so I'm the person who knows them. I'd also ask the hospital volunteer office about a placement, to get a foot in the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but busy. When I've a list, I can manage it. When I've nothing to do, I start doing sums about my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long can you manage on benefits only if nothing comes up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Technically for as long as they pay out, but that's not the same as managing. I'd stop buying anything that isn't food or heat, and I'd start asking my mum to cook for two. The benefit rules also say I must keep looking, so there's pressure to take whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take if nothing in health admin came up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything with people: a shop, a call centre, even school lunches. I wouldn't love a call centre, because that's the exact work AI takes first. But I'd rather have a wage and keep looking from inside, than stay at home waiting.

say: I'd say admin and **front-desk workers** are hit first, and retraining needs a **stipend**.
I'd tell office friends to learn the tools **before their boss** does it for them.
think: Receptionist jobs get **thinner** each year, with more applicants for fewer roles.
Clinics still need someone who can **calm a frightened patient**.
do: Widen the search to **clinical support** and practice coordinator roles.
Take a short course on practice-management software and learn AI **scheduling tools**.
Ask the hospital volunteer office about a **placement**.
feel: Anxious but busy, and when I've nothing to do I do **sums** about my rent.
S1.quote: I'd rather have a wage and keep looking from inside, than stay at home waiting.
fieldNote: Reads the scenario through her own **front-desk experience**.
Willing to take a call centre job, knowing it is the work **AI takes first**.
Alarmed because her whole role type shrinks and her cushion is nil.

steps.text: Apply for clinical support and practice coordinator jobs at the hospital
Take a short course on practice-management software
Learn an AI scheduling tool by booking mock appointments
Ask the hospital volunteer office about a placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. I'd find it hard to believe, but I'd also feel I couldn't take the chance that it's not true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that if this is coming in two years, governments must start work today on income support and retraining. I'd write to my MP and say people like me need a plan, not a slogan. I'd also say that no company should be allowed to lay off thousands overnight without notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be overtaken before I finish my certificate. Anything that's desk-based, mine included, would be done by software that's better and cheaper. I'd keep trying, but I'd be one of a very big crowd in a very small queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the long courses and go for quick, cheap things that get me paid soon, such as care-assistant or school support work, which need people. I'd tell the council and the jobcentre early, so I'm first in line for any scheme. I'd cut my spending to the bone, and I'd ask my mum if I could move back in if the rent became impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, in a quiet way. I'd stop sleeping properly. I'd keep telling myself to take it one day at a time, which is just a way of not looking at the whole thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How hard would moving back in with your mum be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard, because I'm thirty-four and I like my own front door. But my mum would have me, and it would cut out rent. I'd see moving back as a pause, not a failure, though I'd probably cry a bit in the car on the way there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the three years before robots reach hands-on work change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It nudges me towards care and school support, since those need a human for longer. But I wouldn't trust that, because I've seen jobs vanish before anyone warned me. I'd say it's a small cushion, not a safe harbour.

I'd write to my **MP** and ask for a plan, not a slogan.
think: I'd be overtaken **before my certificate** is finished.
I'd be one of a **big crowd** in a very small queue.
do: Skip long courses and go for quick, **cheap routes** into care or school support.
Tell the council and jobcentre early to get **first in line** for schemes.
Ask my mum about **moving back in** if rent becomes impossible.
feel: Frightened in a quiet way, and **not sleeping** properly.
S2.quote: I'd see moving back as a pause, not a failure, though I'd probably cry a bit in the car on the way there.
fieldNote: Considers **moving back** with her mother, with pride and sadness both showing.
Trusts nothing about timing: jobs have vanished **without warning** before.
Her plan shifts to **quick routes** into work over long courses.

steps.text: Apply for care assistant and school support jobs within the month
Register early with the council and jobcentre for every support scheme
Cut spending to rent, heat, food and travel only
Move back in with my mum if the rent becomes impossible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to do something, though it's not a cosy amount of time. At least it's not two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we have to choose the safety net now: retraining that pays a wage, health and care jobs funded, and some kind of income floor. I'd say we can't wait until the damage is done. I'd vote for whoever takes it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I can do two things in that time. Finish my certificate and get into a healthcare admin role, then learn the systems enough to move to a coordinator or support job that sits above the software. I wouldn't be sure, but it feels doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd complete the course and apply to hospital trusts and GP groups, then take any job and learn the practice systems fast. I'd save a small amount each month, even twenty pounds, in a separate account. I'd use the AI tools more and more, because eventually the people who can manage them will be the ones who keep a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously okay. It's like when the dentist says it won't hurt much, and you believe him about seventy percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this feel different from the 2028 version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I was scrambling to survive. In 2031 I can still make a plan and finish things. That sounds small, but the difference is between running and walking fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think will do best in five years, and who worst?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The best will be people who learn the systems and still have a human touch, like nurses with good tech skills. The worst will be those who only did one job for twenty years and have no way to change, like some of the receptionists I knew. I'd like to be in the first group, but I'm not sure.

say: I'd say we must choose the **safety net** now, with retraining that pays a wage.
I'd say we can't wait until the **damage** is done.
think: I can **finish my certificate** and move into healthcare admin, then above the software.
It feels **doable**, though I'm not sure.
do: Complete the course and apply to **hospital trusts** and GP groups.
Save even **twenty pounds** a month in a separate account.
Use AI tools more, so I can **manage** them.
feel: Cautiously okay, like believing the dentist about **seventy percent**.
S3.quote: In 2028 I was scrambling to survive. In 2031 I can still make a plan and finish things.
fieldNote: Describes the time gap as **running versus walking fast**.
Sees a niche in being the one who **manages the tools**.
Humour and caution together; the plan is realistic, not rosy.

steps.text: Complete the medical-administration certificate and apply to hospital trusts
Take the first healthcare admin job and learn the practice systems
Save twenty pounds a month in a separate account
Use AI tools weekly to practise scheduling and drafting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives real space. I'll be forty-four, still working, with time to try a second path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time if we use it wisely, with proper training funds, decent pay for caring and clinical work, and honest planning from government. I'd also say people should be told plainly what's coming and not fobbed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I can manage ten years. I'd get a job in healthcare admin, then train further, perhaps as a practice manager or a clinical coordinator. My worry is that I'm starting from zero cash, so any bad month could knock the plan sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate, get a job, and then take a part-time diploma in healthcare management. I'd save regularly and aim for a three-month cushion within two years. I'd keep using AI tools and maybe start tutoring older patients on how to use their phones, since I've always been good at patient explanations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a note of worry underneath. Ten years feels manageable, but my wallet doesn't agree with my optimism yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do with a first wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down the little debt on my phone and start the cushion. Then I'd buy a proper winter coat, which I've put off for three years. I'd also take my mum out for a Sunday roast, because she's earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in year eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the healthcare jobs also change faster than we thought, and that I'd be forty-two with a certificate nobody needs. I'd want to keep learning every year so I'm never caught flat. A steady habit of learning beats one big course, I think.

say: I'd say ten years is good if we use it for **training funds** and decent care pay.
I'd say people should be told **plainly** what's coming.
think: I can manage ten years: healthcare admin first, then **practice manager** training.
I start from **zero cash**, so a bad month could knock the plan sideways.
do: Finish the certificate, get a job, then take a part-time **healthcare management** diploma.
Aim for a **three-month cushion** within two years.
Start tutoring older patients on their **phones**.
feel: Fairly calm with a **note of worry**, since my wallet doesn't agree with my optimism.
S4.quote: I'd want to keep learning every year so I'm never caught flat. A steady habit of learning beats one big course, I think.
fieldNote: Time lets her plan a **ladder**: admin, diploma, practice manager.
Her patient-explaining skill becomes a **side idea**.
Anxious because zero cash makes any bad month dangerous.

steps.text: Finish the certificate and take a healthcare admin job
Study a part-time healthcare management diploma in the evenings
Build a three-month cushion within two years of working
Tutor older patients on using their phones for small fees

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be racing the clock with nothing in the bank and my kind of job at the front of the line. What would help is retraining that pays something, jobs in care or health with a real future, and an honest warning from the government before it all lands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not a drama person. I don't panic easily, and I'm still frightened by two years. Please make it clear that ordinary, sensible people feel this way too.

headlineQuote: I'm not a drama person. I don't panic easily, and I'm still frightened by two years.
portrait: Sara is **34**, lives alone above a hairdresser's in Eldermoor, and has been on **benefits only** since May.
She spent nine years running a dental practice's front desk until a **dental group** moved the work to a central team.
She uses AI tools now and then, but keeps her **own plain voice**.
She stays practical and balanced, blames consolidation more than technology, and is **alarmed** when her whole job type shrinks.
With more time she plans a ladder from health admin to **practice management**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd race the clock with nothing in the bank.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining that pays** something and jobs in care or health with a real future.
An **honest warning** from government before it lands.
